blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Your Honour, your Lordship, I will just be sitting behind the prosecutor to translate everything to him in English to be sure that he's understood everything thoroughly. Just to let you know.
blocks.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Good morning, members of the jury. I'm sorry you've been delayed in being brought into court.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

It is a requirement of Swiss law, as I understand it, that when a witness gives evidence in Switzerland in relation to any proceedings in another jurisdiction, although the Swiss have no interest in the proceedings because it does not affect them, there requires to be a translation of the proceedings into French because it's a French-speaking part of Switzerland, so there is, just off screen to your left, someone who will be translating when required or interpreting into French and back into English. But the prosecutor has told me he can understand English, so there should be in difficulty or hindrance in that respect. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Otherwise the proceedings are just as if the witness was here in England. Sometimes witnesses do appear remotely from places in the United Kingdom and when that happens juries are told, as I direct you, to attach no significance to the fact that the witness is not present in court but is giving evidence remotely over the link.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just as I've said in relation to all witnesses, you regard the status of the witness as exactly the same whether they're present in court or appearing remotely or, if they are in court, they're screened from anyone and attach no significance that Dr Rylance, who lives and works in Switzerland, is not here but is in Switzerland when she is giving her evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

DR SARAH RYLANCE (affirmed)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Dr Rylance, could I invite you to state your name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. My name is Sarah Jane Rylance.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Can you see me clearly or would it be better if I stood to address you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think I can see you. Are you the gentleman in the middle of the front row?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I'll stand to my feet now. Is that more clear?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Dr Rylance, I understand that you were employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital in June 2015; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: What was your professional status at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I was a registrar working at the hospital.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: We understand that you worked a long day shift on Saturday, 20 June 2015; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. That is what I have written in my statement, which was prepared from the medical notes, so yes, I would agree.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Dr Rylance, I'm going to direct your attention, if I may, to clinical notes compiled in relation to a patient called [Baby D]. Do you confirm that you have those clinical notes in front of you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I have some clinical notes here.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. If we look at the pagination in the bottom right corner, I think the first page of notes on this particular baby is numbered page number 9. Do you have that? For our purposes, it's behind tile 14.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My pages seem to start at... Are you referring to the most -- the number at the bottom right-hand corner?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have page 11. The part marked up for me as clinical notes starts at page 11.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Dr Rylance, is that an entry in your handwriting, dated 20 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. Page 11 starts with the writing of one of my colleagues and it doesn't have a date on it. I think...
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I don't think I have... I'm just looking through all of the other pages. This has just been given to me recently, but I don't have... I don't have a page 9 with my writing on from that date.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Dr Rylance, you do have a copy of your witness statement; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I do have a copy of my witness statement, yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Could you give me one second, please, Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)

In the absence of the relevant corresponding clinical notes, I'll take you through the part of your statement where you state that you had the opportunity to review the notes and you give a history of your involvement with [Baby D] on Saturday 20 June 2015.
Okay.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: But before we do that, could you take one more look through those clinical notes and see whether you have an entry in your handwriting, dated 20 June?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: (Pause)
Dr Rylance, can you see images on a screen?

Yes, I can. So that is my writing, yes. I think the notes that I have here, they start with my colleague's notes, which subsequently -- they're from the evening or the night of the 20th. So I think I'm missing that page there that you're showing me, but I can read my writing fairly clearly on the screen.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I'm grateful. We'll use the screen-projected note if we may.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a note recorded by you on 20 June, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Is it a note that first sets out some information about the baby that was recorded immediately after her birth?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Were you present at her birth or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not that I recall. I think -- so I'm only really able to go on what I've written in the notes, given the time that's passed. The fact that I've written "written in retrospect" and I've put that information there, if I'd been present at the birth I'm sure that I would have documented in the notes sooner than that. So I don't believe I was at the birth, no.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: The information that you've recorded there sets out the time of the birth, her birth weight, and some of the details that pertain to her condition at birth. Is it your evidence that they were facts reported to you by somebody else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, they would either have been reported to me by someone or I would have taken them from entries earlier on in the medical notes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. If I ask Mr Murphy here in court in Manchester to allow us to look further down the note, please. Pausing there, we'll see an entry in your hand that begins with the words:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Bleeped again as midwife not happy with her colour."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you see those words, Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Does this record that you were bleeped to attend upon the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you scroll up a little bit so I can see what came immediately before?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Immediately before:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Reviewed at 1.5 hours by SHO."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You were not an SHO at this point, you were a registrar?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Grunting but otherwise [I can't read your handwriting] obs..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that "okay and examined normally"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct. So where I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Bleeped again as midwife not happy with her."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I am not able to say whether that was me that was bleeped again or whether that was the SHO that was bleeped again. From what I have written there, I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Understood. The next entry reads:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Brought [that is the baby] to unit for screen."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does it read:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On arrival to neonatal unit, looked dusky, poor respiratory"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Are you able to say whether those facts were facts observed by you or facts reported to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, those would be facts observed by me.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll proceed on the basis that the rest of this record are facts observed by you unless you tell us otherwise. Do you understand?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I'm very grateful.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So could you help us with the next paragraph of recorded notes, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Initial saturations 48%."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: This is the oxygen saturations:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Poor respiratory effort at about 7.30 pm. The baby was transferred into an incubator and given IPPV."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: This is intermittent positive pressure ventilation, what we call bagging, with the Neopuff, so to try and stimulate her with her breathing:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "She pinked up quickly [so her colour was better] and started regular resps."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: That means regular respiration, regular breathing.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. So they record your efforts to stimulate the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Were those efforts successful or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, from -- so she gained more colour and started breathing regularly, so yes, they were successful.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you take us through the next part of the note, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have written "IV access obtained". That means intravenous access, so we put a cannula into her hand or foot. And then I've written the investigations which were taken. "Culture" is a blood culture, full blood count and CRP, which is a marker of inflammation. BM4.2 is her blood glucose level. And then at the time that we put the cannula in, we also take a sample from the blood which is called a blood gas and then the next -- the numbers there are related to the result from the blood gas that was taken.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you able to provide us with an assessment as to the baby's condition based on your interpretation of that data recorded in that paragraph?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So in terms of her clinical condition, she's responded well to the ventilatory support she's been given and has had a good response to that. Relating to the blood gas results, it's difficult to say how that reflects her clinical condition. So it's part of a number of things that we look at when we are making an assessment but it's not the only thing we would look at. So the blood gas, the numbers parameters in the blood gas reading are abnormal. They suggest that she has had some difficulty with her respiratory system, with her breathing, and also from her -- there is a metabolic component to the blood gas that is abnormal.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: But I wouldn't use a blood gas in itself to make a clinical assessment, I think it's done in combination with her -- the rest of the clinical examination.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we move to the final paragraph on page 9? What does that inform us of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've written "IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin given", with a tick, which means I gave intravenous antibiotics, two antibiotics into the cannula that I'd just put in. She's transferred on to CPAP. CPAP is continuous positive airway pressure. It's a form of ventilatory support which is given to try and help babies to breathe and that will have been done because she had initially poor respiratory effort and although she has pinked up in response to the stimulation that she was given, I think we felt that she needed to have ongoing respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Then I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "IV bolus 0.9% NaCl."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which is a bolus of normal saline through the cannula we've put in. I've documented the amount that we've given. So we give 10ml of fluid for every kg and she weighed 3.1 kilos, so she was given 31ml of fluid.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we scroll further down the page, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Could you continue to interpret the notes for us then, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly. So I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Gas bili on exchange line."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: That means that on the gas -- the blood gas sample that was taken, the bilirubin level -- bili is bilirubin, when we're -so bilirubin is a chemical that we find in the blood and in jaundiced babies and in order to decide what kind of treatment is needed we have a graph that we look at, which has various different lines on it in terms of what intervention would be needed, so whether they might need phototherapy to correct their jaundice.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So when I have written "on exchange line", what it means is that there is a line on that graph that would suggest that she might need to have an exchange transfusion if her jaundice continued to develop. So in order to try and prevent that, because that's quite an extreme form of therapy and this is the first time that
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: we have checked her bilirubin level, we've started her on -- the photo of me in the room I'm in is blocking a little bit -- I think it says, "Started on triple", I imagine it says phototherapy --
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Lights."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Lights? Okay. So the phototherapy lights that we use to treat jaundice, you can use one set, two sets or three sets. So we've started her on the maximum treatment to try and bring that bilirubin level down.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move to the next paragraph. It begins with the words, I think, "Currently on CPAP".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm documenting then -- so at that point we've moved her on to the CPAP machine, which was started at 8 o'clock in the evening, and the number 6 centimetres of water refers to the pressure of the CPAP machine, she's in 40% oxygen, and her own oxygen saturations that we monitor on babies on the neonatal unit are 100%, which is --
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So -- you continue, please, Dr Rylance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the next -- my next documentation is my clinical examination of her. So "HS1 plus 2 plus 0" means her heart sounds were normal. CR is capillary refill, which was less than 2 seconds, which is normal. I felt for her femoral pulses -- so "femoral tick tick" means that both her femoral pulses were present. "P135" is her pulse rate, which is okay. Then I've written she has -- her chest is clear, she has regular respiratory effort, but fairly shallow breathing, her abdomen is soft and not distended, she has normal -- N in a circle -- is normal female genitalia and a normal anus. So this is my first complete examination of her that I've documented there and everything in that examination is normal.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So the plan --
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Yes, go on, tell us about the plan.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So at that time the plan I've documented is to continue on CPAP, on the breathing support, and then to continue with intravenous fluids. So I've written 10% DEX, which is dextrose, at 60ml/kg/day -- again, this is the way we calculate the amount of fluids based on their weight.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So she was given a normal saline bolus on the previous page of 31ml and that's given as a push, we would give that through quickly, and then we've connected her up to her a set that will continue to run with dextrose.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And then the plan at that point was to repeat the gas, the blood gas, at 8.45.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Then at 20.20, did you record the explanation that you provided to little [Baby D]'s parents?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Parents updated, explained likely sepsis."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which is another word for infection:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Needing help with breathing."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: She's on the CPAP, the respiratory support at present:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "She may need further support with her ventilation and she was receiving antibiotics [ABX is antibiotics] to treat infection."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: What was the basis of your conclusion of "likely sepsis"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think that in the background details that I've recorded that there'd been a prolonged rupture of membranes and I think given that otherwise there was nothing particular to explain her condition, the most likely cause for a baby of that size and gestation to be born and have difficulty, as she seemed to be having with her breathing and with the abnormal parameters on her blood gas, would be infection.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. What, if any, view did you form as to her clinical condition or clinical progress from the time that she'd been admitted on to the neonatal unit until this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think she had responded well to the interventions that we had done. She had responded well to the respiratory stimulation that she'd been given and appeared to be stable, to have stabilised on the CPAP, and was making respiratory efforts for herself. So I think overall I would say that I was happy with the progress since she was admitted, although she'd obviously need to be closely -- continue to be closely monitored and assessed.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder whether we could go down to the next page, please. We'll see entries made by a colleague of yours. If we go to the bottom of that page -- no, that's the extent of your entries on that page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I wonder whether we could show the doctor page 15 of the clinical notes, which are at our J2220, which are, amongst other places, tile 133.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have page 15 with me here if that's helpful.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: It is very helpful. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, sorry, that's not the same as page 15 that I have.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Okay, fine, that is the page 15 that I have, yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Good. This records an entry made by you at 14.00 hours the following day, that is to say Sunday, 21 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Does this entry at 14.00 hours record your insertion of a UAC and UVC into [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Could you take us through this entry then, please, Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly. So I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "UAC [which is an umbilical arterial catheter] and UVC [umbilical venous catheter] inserted under aseptic technique."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "UVC only able to advance to 5 centimetres, removed."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Do you want me to explain what I mean by what I've written?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So usually if you are inserting a UVC, you expect to be able to advance it much further than 5 centimetres, you're feeding it in through the umbilical vein, and it should go in more than 5 centimetres. Sometimes it can be quite fiddly and difficult to do these procedures in newborn babies. It's not uncommon that it's not successful and so if it was only able to go into 5 centimetres it means probably the catheter was actually barely beyond the umbilical stump and actually into the baby. So it was removed because it was not successful.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Then I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "UAC inserted to 20.5 centimetres as per calculation."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Again, there is a way that we calculate how far to feed the catheter into the baby based on the baby's weight. So I have inserted it to the distance that I would expect to. It wasn't sampling back -- so when you put the catheter in, normally you then expect to be able to draw back and get a blood sample and it didn't sample back.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: We do an X-ray to check the position of the catheters when we put them in and I have written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "On X-ray in way too far. Route not typical of UAC.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Therefore pulled back until sampling at 9 centimetres."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So I think -- what I think there or my interpretation of what I've written there is that normally you look at the way the catheter -- you look at how the -- the appearance of the catheter on the X-ray and it should follow a particular route according to the blood vessels. What I was thinking there, I think, is it wasn't actually in the umbilical artery, it was in the umbilical vein instead, and therefore it wasn't in the correct position and I have pulled it back until I was able to get a blood sample from it.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: The next comment is:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Gas much improved."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Again, the numbers there reflect the blood gas measurements that we look at. I've circled "PO2 7.1".
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: This is the amount of oxygen in the blood and the fact that this is a low level, so it would suggest that again the catheter is in a vein and not in the artery.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Then I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Re-X-rayed. Position looks better on machine.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Awaiting Meditech upload to view and measure more accurately. [Query] still not typical course. Can connect to transducer for [blood pressure] monitoring."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: What this means is that when the -- on the neonatal unit, because the babies are sick, we are not able to take them somewhere to get a formal X-ray done, and so at the point at which we've put the umbilical lines in, we would arrange for a technician to come and do an X-ray on the unit. We can then review the X-ray on the actual X-ray machine. It's not as clear as looking at it on a computer screen afterwards but it's useful
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: at the time in order to be able to make faster decisions or assessments. So that's what I mean when I said that the position looks better on the machine, but we are waiting for it to be uploaded onto the system so we can look at it properly on a computer screen.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Going back to the part of your note where you record "gas much improved", what was the point of comparison there? Much improved from what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I assume that it is improved from the previous gas reading. I'm looking now at -- trying... So I don't know what the previous -- but normally you would just be comparing the trends with the previous gases. I assume it's related to the gas.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue down the page then, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you see an X-ray review stamp of an X-ray taken at 13.46? Is that a repetition of the information you've just shared with us or is this additional to it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I think this is repetition. On the neonatal unit each time we take an X-ray to look at the line positions, we would put this sticker in the note. So this is really duplicating, effectively, what I've written earlier in that. It looks like the umbilical arterial catheter is actually in the umbilical vein and so it was pulled back. So then what is left is a catheter that's in the umbilical vein, not in the artery.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue down the page where you then record your plan at this point in time, which was, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plan was to continue on the CPAP, so on the ventilatory support, but in air, so she wasn't needing any additional oxygen at that time, the machine is just providing some pressure but not extra oxygen to her, and to repeat a blood gas at 6.30. And then the plan was also to try and take -- again to take some blood back from the UVC, the umbilical venous catheter, so we could check another blood gas and the bilirubin and U&E, which is urea and electrolytes, and CRP, which is an inflammatory marker.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. I expect, if we continue down the page, we'll see your notes of a review of the baby at 19.00 hours that Sunday evening.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I've got that page.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: We have "Day 2 of life" and her gestational age. Then we have your notes that begin with the words "Presumed sepsis, CRP 1"; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Help us: expand on CRP 1 for us and its significance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: CRP 1 is the C-reactive protein. It's a marker we check in babies when we think there may be infection. 1 is a normal value it's not raised. That doesn't necessarily mean that the baby doesn't have sepsis.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Sometimes there is a delay in the inflammatory markers rising, given that she's still quite -- that she's only on her second day of life at this point. Even though her CRP is normal at that point, we would still continue to be suspicious of and treat for infection.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Then I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "On CPAP [so she was still on respiratory support] having been extubated at 9 am."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: This document is at 7 in the evening. So it looks like she's been on CPAP for the whole of the day.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: We previously saw a note that recorded a CRP level of 6 and now 1. Would you have attached any significance to that change in data or is it not possible to form conclusions drawn from those facts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I wouldn't be particularly... I wouldn't attach particular significance to those, I think a CRP of 1 is low, a CRP of 6, it's also low. I'd have to -- I think the normal range for a CRP is less than 10. It does vary from hospital to hospital and I can't remember, given the time now, what the normal range was in Chester at the time. But I think both of the values are fairly low, but still, as I said before, based on her clinical condition, even with those results, we would continue to treat for infection.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Understood. Your next sub-paragraph is under the heading "Vent", is that ventilation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is ventilation, yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Could you read and expand upon the next entry for us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure. I've written "CPAP 6 centimetres", so it's -- 6 centimetres is the amount of water pressure that's been used in the CPAP machine. I've documented that she's been in air all day, she's saturating well. By "in air" I mean that although she's on the CPAP to support her breathing, she's not needed any additional oxygen all day:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Saturating well. No desaturations."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Her initial gases after extubation, which was earlier in the morning, were not good. Her pH was 7.1 and her pCO2 was 9, therefore she had been put on to CPAP rather than left without any ventilatory support.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So reading this, she'd been extubated at 9, then put on to CPAP at 10.30 in the morning, and then subsequent gases, so the gas from the UVC that I'd taken was good.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I've documented that gas there, which is a big improvement on the previous gas.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Reviewing those entries from the point of extubation at 9 am, the intervention at 10.30 am, and these gases reviewed at 18.45 hours, is that right, the last time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: What was your appraisal of her state in terms of her respiration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think from a respiratory perspective she appears to have made good progress during the day. She's moved from requiring ventilation the previous night, she's tolerated extubation, and she's needed minimal respiratory support. That CPAP pressure is not high and she's not needed any oxygen and her blood gases show an improvement. So I think her ventilatory status was very satisfactory at the point at which I reviewed her.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Can we move on to fluids, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Fluids. On 75ml/kg/day of 10% dextrose."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Again this is calculating how much fluid she needs based on her weight. This is a standard amount:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "She had a 10ml/kg normal saline bolus at 11 am due to rising lactate and slightly delayed capillary refill."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So this was a bolus of fluid that was given earlier on in the day to try and improve her perfusion. And then I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Just passed first urine, 13ml."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which is an encouraging sign, it shows that she's able to pass urine.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: BM is her blood glucose, which is 7.1, which is okay. And BP, her blood pressure, is now 60/39.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: How would you evaluate that blood pressure reading?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's difficult to take in the context of a single reading. I think that -- to me that seems unremarkable.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Let's move on then. Sorry, you continue, Dr Rylance, my apologies.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was going to say, usually for newborn babies we have charts where we can look to check the normal parameters, again based on their size. I can't remember off the top of my head what those parameters would be, but I'm sure if I'd been concerned by the blood pressure reading I would have made a comment.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next sub-paragraph then, sepsis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Sepsis. Initial CRP 1."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So the CRP result from the first blood sample that was taken was 1. And then a repeat CRP just taken. So I think at that point I'd taken another sample from her UVC:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Not had LP yet."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: LP is a lumbar puncture. So in babies where we have concerns about infection, if we think that they are clinically stable, we often would choose to do a lumbar puncture to make sure that the infection hasn't spread into their spinal fluid and around their brain. But she hadn't been stable enough to have had that done at that point.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. The next paragraph, is that an abbreviation for "on examination"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: How was she on examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would you like me to take you through the whole documentation?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Responsive on handling."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which is a good sign:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "No abnormal movements."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Her tone was reasonable:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Heart sound 1 plus 2 plus 0."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which was normal:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Capillary refill less than 2 seconds."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Which is normal:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Femoral pulses tick tick."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So both still palpable. Pulse rate is 130 which is unremarkable:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Chest clear. Regular respiratory effort. Minimal recession."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So recession is what we look for to see whether babies are struggling with their breathing and the fact there was minimal recession is positive, a good sign:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Abdomen was soft, not distended. She has an umbilical venous catheter which is secured at 6 centimetres. Normal female genitalia. Feet quite purple and bruised, but capillary refill is less than 2 seconds."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: She will have had quite a lot of samples taken from her feet. We do heel prick sampling in newborn babies, so sometimes they can have quite bruised feet, so that's what that is referring to.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So overall from the --
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Yes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Overall from my examination there, I would say that she was stable and she was handling well and that she had been sort
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: of responding well during the day. This is a satisfactory examination.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Responding well, responding to what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To the treatment that she'd had over the course of the day in terms of the antibiotics, the fluids, the minimal respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Just to go back to one aspect of your note, "Tone reasonable". Could you expand upon that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sure. So one of the things that I would look at if I was assessing a baby is how they're handling. So the tone is whether they might be very floppy and limp or, if you're looking on the other side, to see if they're too stiff or if they're having any abnormal movements.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Her tone was reasonable, so that suggests to me that she wasn't particularly floppy, that she was -- I've written she was responsive on handling, so she was moving like I would expect a normal baby to.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go to what I think is the penultimate paragraph. What does that abbreviation stand for in the left margin?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Imp" stands for impression. This is the impression that sums up sort of the assessment that I've laid out.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So I have written she's stable on CPAP, we tried taking her off but her respiratory effort became irregular and she desaturated a few times so she was put back on.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: What if any significance, clinical significance, would you or did you attach to the fact that her respiratory effort became irregular when first taken off CPAP?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I wouldn't have attached a lot of significance to it.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I think given that she was extubated earlier that morning, it takes babies some time to settle and she was obviously unwell when she came round to the neonatal unit on the previous evening, so I think I would have interpreted that as that she just needed a bit more time, a bit more support in terms of her -- from the CPAP in terms of respiratory support, just to -yes, just to allow her to transition from having been ventilated and then moving to breathing for herself in the day.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So we usually try to move the babies forward by taking them off the CPAP but if they don't seem to tolerate it well or we have
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: any concerns, we can just put them back on and give them a bit more time. So I would have -- to me I would just interpret that as that she needed a bit more time on the respiratory support, but that she was heading in the right direction since she wasn't needing any oxygen on it, she was just needing the pressure from the machine without any additional oxygen.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So your plan was to leave on CPAP, await further results; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So we were repeating -- we just repeated the CRP, the infection marker, U&Es, urea and electrolytes, and bilirubin level, to leave the umbilical venous catheter in, so that we could sample for gases from it, to save having to keep pricking her heels, which I've commented were quite bruised, and continue on the antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: ABX is antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Taking a step back if you would, you've examined this baby and considered data that was obtained in relation to this baby twice in the space of about 24 hours, Saturday night and Sunday night; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Firstly, as of this final set of observations on the Sunday night, what was your assessment as to her clinical condition?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was happy with her clinical condition. I think on the basis of this review, which I've done towards the end of my shift, before handing over to my colleague, that she's had a very satisfactory day. Generally, she has been improving in terms of needing less respiratory support, handling well. She was a good colour, she wasn't needing any oxygen. Clinically, I would say I'd be very happy with her from that assessment and that she'd shown a good improvement from the condition which I saw her when I first admitted her to the neonatal unit on the previous evening.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Rylance. That's all the questions I have for you, but my colleague Mr Myers will have some questions for you now.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Can you see me and hear me, please?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. You told us -- there's two occasions when you examined [Baby D] -- two occasions where you were involved: one on 20 June, after her birth. That's the first, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And then you were also involved with her during the day of 21 June and into that evening; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: All right, thank you. You told us that when you left her on 20 June, the first occasion, you were happy with her condition -- happy with her progress, I should say.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Happy with her progress. We'll look a little more closely at what happened when you were with her, but putting the word "happy" to one side, would you have recognised at that time that she was at risk of respiratory complications?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On the first night that she was admitted to the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Yes, and when you came to leave her on that night.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. As I said, she had responded well to what had been done, if you like, when we admitted her to the unit in terms of giving her some puffs with the Neopuff and then putting her on to the CPAP. But her gas wasn't in the normal range and she needed closer monitoring and that's what would have been handed over to my colleague.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Who was Dr Brunton, we've heard?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, from the notes, and I do remember Andrew.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I just want to look at the position then leading up to that, if you could help me with this. We've got the clinical notes, which we refer to as either 2214 or slide 18, but they were put up on the screen, so it might help if we could put them back on the screen, Mr Murphy. It's our slide 18 and it was the first page of Dr Rylance's notes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This should come up on the screen, Dr Rylance.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see those?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I just want to keep the picture in mind. We know that [Baby D]'s mother, [Mother of Baby D], her membranes had been broken or ruptured 60 hours before the time of birth.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are you aware of that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From what I've written in the notes, yes, I can see that I've documented that.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: The notes say "Apgars 8 and 9"; can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: On the face of it, 8 and 9 are relatively good Apgar scores, aren't they? That's, I think, at 5 and at 10 minutes, in fact.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes (inaudible: distorted).
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: We can also see that, within 12 minutes, [Baby D] was in her dad's arms, had lost colour, was floppy and needed five rescue breaths; do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Do you agree that is a worrying sign at that stage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Just pausing there, it would suggest that whatever the Apgars were at 8 and 9, they're not much help in predicting what's going to happen 12 minutes later, are they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think that's fair.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Just so we can keep in mind the picture, we've heard evidence from [Baby D]'s mother, [Mother of Baby D], and she said this about the time we're looking at. She was asked did she see [Baby D] when [Baby D] was delivered and lifted over the screen for her to see, and [Mother of Baby D] said yes. She was asked what impression did she have of [Baby D]'s state, and she said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Not alive, she seemed very lifeless, she didn't scream. There was no sound."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that fits with the period we have at 12 minutes of age:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "In dad's arms, lost colour and floppy."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I ask, when we move forwards and you give us your views of [Baby D]'s condition, what you're happy about, how well she's doing, are you giving us those views by reference to the very poor starting point she had soon after delivery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am giving -- so when I'm talking about how -- my opinion of her at the end of my shift on the day of [Baby D]'s birth, my reference point is the point at which I first had contact with her on the neonatal unit, when she was requiring additional Neopuff respiratory support, and I've documented that her oxygen saturations were, I think, 48%.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: I wasn't at her birth and I wasn't involved with her at this early stage, so I can't comment on how she looked at that time. What I've written there is based on what either I would have been told by colleagues or what I would have taken from others' documentation in the notes. This is, if you like, my summary when I first met [Baby D] to try and put together why she is in the -- how she is and what I need to know in order to move forward with my assessment. So it's like it's my summary but it's not my observations, if that makes sense.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So is it fair to say that the assessments you make of [Baby D] are relative to the starting point that you understood her to come from?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The assessments that I've made are relative to my first assessment of her when she came to the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: If we just look on through those notes, the fact you've written it down means this is material that, if you didn't receive it first-hand, was at least reported to you; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And even if you don't receive it first-hand, you will keep in mind, won't you, material and observations from other practitioners that are reported to you or that is reported to you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So you will have known from the history that she, as we can see reading on, started grunting in theatre.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that, Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Reviewed at 1.5 hours by senior house officer.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Grunting but otherwise obs okay. Examined normally."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Pausing there, grunting like that can mean an indication of a respiratory effort and some difficulty in respiratory effort, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it can.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: If we look on:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bleeped again as midwife not happy with her colour.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Lack of response to vitamin K. Poor feeding."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Brought to unit [is that the neonatal unit?] for screen."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "On arrival at the unit, looked dusky, poor respiratory."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This takes us up to about the point when you become personally directly involved with [Baby D], doesn't it, Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So my -- I'm unable to recollect whether I saw [Baby D] before she came to the unit. I definitely will have admitted her to the unit myself, so where I've written:
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: "Brought to the unit for screen. On arrival looked dusky."
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: This is my observation.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But I don't believe that I was involved in reviewing her before she came to the unit. My supposition is that I would have asked the senior house officer, who had reviewed her, to bring her round directly to the unit when he or the midwife had discussed with me. But from the point at which she came to the unit, these are my direct observations.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Right. We know she was born at 4.01. It has here, where your observations appear, and I'll come to them shortly, we can see there's an arrow and it says 19.30.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Initial sats 48%. Poor respiratory effort 19.30."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Does that mean when you reviewed her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think so.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So you will have reviewed her approximately 3.5 hours after her birth?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And by that time, she's presenting as a baby that is seriously ill, in fact; would you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. From the way that she behaved when she came round to the unit, she was an unwell baby.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: She was an unwell baby. And you put there:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Initial sats 48%, poor respiratory effort, put into the incubator."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you did?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Did you review her at any point that evening when she was with her mother or did you see her after she'd left her mother?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that the first time that I reviewed the baby was when she came to the neonatal unit. I think if I had reviewed her on the ward, I would have documented that in the notes because that would be a reason to document.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: So from what I've -- reading my notes, I think the first time that I reviewed the baby was on the neonatal unit when she was brought around.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: Thank you. If we just move on, on this particular page, Dr Rylance, to the next paragraph in fact. It's got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "IV access obtained."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then we've got:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Culture. FBC, CRP taken. BM 4.2."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I want to ask you, where it says "Venous gas at 19.47", those readings indicate marked acidosis, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: In particular we know that pH should really be in the range of 7.3 to 7.35, and this is low, 7.105, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: That's acidic. And the other readings as well. The carbon dioxide is high, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: RYLANCE

blocks.text: And the base excess is below what you'd regard as the acceptable range?

However, the ITU guidelines are quite specific, so in terms of looking after a baby who's ITU because they're ventilated or on multiple inotropes, obviously that is a much bigger workload for one nurse than having a baby who's got an umbilical line in. While that baby needs close attention, it's a different level of care, but it still comes under ITU.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But certainly if we go from what the guidance is, it should really be one-to-one for [Baby D] and that nurse only looking after [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: That would be the ideal, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to go through what you've said about the night in question, you were asked, as a preliminary question, about whether or not it was quieter at night.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think you said in terms of number of doctors and auxiliary staff there may be fewer of them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of the babies, generally speaking, their needs might apply whatever time of day or night, mightn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Um... Yes. Um... If -- yes, but there will be routine things that happen during the day that don't happen at night.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But you'd still endeavour to have the right number or nurses to babies at night as you would in the day, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes, the ratios are the same, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to go to what you can help us with in terms of the events in the early hours of the morning of 22 June, I'm going to help, if I may, just to make this clear. In your statement that you made on 7 February 2018 you give times to each of the three incidents that we're looking at.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just to help, the first incident you put at 1.30 in the morning, the second incident at 3 am --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- and the third incident at 3.45.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's you doing your best to put the times on those according to the notes and whatever you can remember --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- 3 years later.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right? Again just so we can be quite clear, there was one occasion, this is a matter of record, on which there was resuscitation, and that was the third occasion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think there was reference made to the first time she was resuscitated but it's one time that resuscitation took place, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: I think so.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The third?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On the first occasion I just want to ask you a little bit about the rash that you've told us about. When you gave evidence about it a few minutes ago, you described it as mottled, white circles with a reddy colour, and you said it was an odd colour, reddy brown. I've summarised it a bit --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- but I've gone to the descriptions you gave of the rash.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When you made the statement what you said, I can show it to you, but perhaps I could read it to you. What you said about it then was:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It was mottled in colour. I'd say it was like circles with a blood supply around them."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You said.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes, mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we can follow, is that how you remembered it when you came to tell the police about two and three-quarter years later or to any extent is that what you had, having spoken to other people and at all been influenced by what they said? If you could help us with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: No, that's how I remember the rash.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: It's not really a rash, but yeah.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of red or reddy-brown, is that something you recall? I only ask because you didn't use the expressions red or reddy-brown in the statement and I just want to ask, is that something you can see in your head now when you look back at it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes, I can remember the --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. And did you see for how long that lasted or are you unable to say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: I can't say that now, I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it's something you certainly saw in whatever period of time you looked at [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: More than that, you just can't say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE C: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. In fact, that's all that I need to ask, [Nurse C]. Thank you very much?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE C: Thank you.

blocks.text: Witness statement of EMILY THOMAS (read)
The first statement is from Emily Thomas.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Emily Thomas signed her witness statement on 21 November 2017. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I qualified as a doctor in 2011 and I have just recently started my fourth year specialist training programme in paediatrics with the intention of becoming a consultant paediatrician."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She says where she's currently working and describes her rotation around the Mersey and North-west Deanery, each 6 months:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I started my paediatric training at Liverpool Women's Hospital in September 2014 and in early March 2015 I transferred to the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: While working at Chester I lived nearby."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: On Sunday, 21 June 2015 I was working on a night shift going into a Monday. I remember the shift was quite busy and I spent a lot of time on the children's ward. Andrew Brunton was the registrar who was working with me. He had been called a couple
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: of times during the night to treat a baby called [Baby D] on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Having refreshed my memory by looking at the notes, I remember [Baby D] had an unusual episode where she came out in a rash. This occurred around 1.30 in the morning. I remember taking a look. I would describe the rash as almost having the appearance of a meningococcal type rash. It was purple in colour and mainly over the abdomen. Andrew called the consultant, Dr Newby, for advice. She came into the unit and reviewed the care and added an extra antibiotic into [Baby D]'s treatment. [Baby D] seemed to settle down and the rash appeared to fade.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "But then later, [Baby D] had another episode where she desaturated and Andrew went to see her again. Around 4.30 in the morning I was on the neonatal unit, I was in either room 2 or 3. I was with another baby that I think needed a septic screen and I was in the middle of trying to insert a cannula or reviewing this baby when I heard a member of staff shouting for help in room number 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I'm not sure but I think the member of staff was a nurse called Lucy. I recall that she had brown hair and was the designated nurse for [Baby D]. This nurse later became very upset in front of me. I believe she had been the designated nurse for [Baby A] who died on the unit only a couple of weeks previously.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think she said something like, 'This is my second baby that this has happened to'.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I ran into room number 1 and there were either one or two nurses already there beside the incubator.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think the nurse that had called for help was bagging [Baby D] because she was struggling to breathe and her oxygen levels had dropped. I could see from the monitors that her oxygen levels were falling and her heart rate was dropping. I asked one of the nurses to put out a crash call to urgently summon the registrar and Dr Brunton arrived shortly afterwards. We started a full resuscitation and she was given adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember Andrew asked a nurse to get the consultant on the phone. I think it was Nurse Kathryn Percival that passed the phone over to him. He explained the situation that he was conducting a full resuscitation. He thought he was talking to Dr Newby but there had been a mix-up and in fact he was talking to [Baby B]'s mother. The mistake was awful and I was completely shocked. [Mother of Babies A & B]'s son, [Baby A], had already died on the unit. Dr Brunton was mortified about the mistake and also shocked when he learnt who was on the phone.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Newby arrived shortly afterwards and [Baby D]'s parents were also called down to the neonatal unit and were present during resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Very sadly, resuscitation attempts were unsuccessful and we eventually stopped after several rounds of adrenaline. I do not recall seeing the rash on [Baby D] during resuscitation attempts and I don't think there were any other babies in room 1 during this time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I later discussed [Baby D]'s treatment with Dr Brunton and he updated her medical notes."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And she describes how, some months later, she moved to Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of ELIZABETH MARSHALL (read)
Moving on, my Lord, to Elizabeth Marshall, who we've heard mentioned. She signed a statement on 18 December 2017. She says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am currently employed at the Countess of Chester Hospital as a band 4 neonatal assistant within the neonatal unit. I have reviewed the nursing notes for [Baby D] to refresh my memory for this interview.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was working a night shift on Sunday, 21 June through to Monday the 22nd. Caroline Oakley, Kate Ward, [Nurse C] and Lucy Letby were all working on the shift. I do not remember who the designated nurse was for [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At this time there was a transitional care system in place. This allowed babies that were premature but did not require monitoring or respiratory assistance to stay with their mother upstairs on the post-natal ward and we would provide assistance with their feeding. On this particular shift I was caring for [and she gives the initials] AH on the post-natal ward and two other babies, IR and NM, on the neonatal unit. Neither of these two babies were located in room 1.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do not remember where I was or how I was informed that [Baby D] had collapsed and was informed that a resuscitation attempt was in progress. When I entered room 1 I saw Lucy Letby giving chest compressions.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Caroline Oakley was present as was Dr Newby, and I think [Nurse C] was also there. There might have been other doctors present as well but I'm not sure. I know Kate Ward was working this shift but I don't recall seeing her at this time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think they took it in turns to carry out the compressions on [Baby D]. I was not directly involved with the resuscitation, my only involvement was that of scribing. Caroline Oakley was shouting out what was going on and what drugs and doses were being administered and I was writing it down.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember I wrote on a paper towel which I later handed to one of the doctors so they could update their notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was in the room for approximately 15 minutes when a decision was made to stop the resuscitation efforts and, sadly, [Baby D] died. I then continued with the care of the babies that I had been allocated.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At the end of the shift the team had a quick meeting to discuss [Baby D] but there was no formal debrief as such and there were no conclusions as to what had happened."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. Just by way of explanation, it was understood that all the questions that were going to be asked of Dr Rylance would have to be translated into French so the prosecutor could understand what the questions were and then the answers that Dr Rylance gave would have to be translated into French as well. You can appreciate that that would have taken at least twice as long as the process in fact took because it was ascertained this morning, before you came into court, by me that everyone could understand English. So there didn't need to be a translation, simultaneous translation, of what took place.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So Dr Rylance's evidence was a lot shorter than was thought was going to be the case and that's the reason we're finishing early this afternoon because witnesses can't just be called from clinical duties now to fill in gaps, I'm afraid. So it means it's an early day for you. But I thought it were better just to read those statements now than for you to have lunch and then come back for 10 minutes, which would have been more of a waste of your time. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that's it for today. We will continue again tomorrow. Remember, of course, your responsibilities as jurors in this case, as I'm sure you do. 10.30 tomorrow morning. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)

Mr Astbury, I didn't raise the matter in front of the jury, but the evidence of Dr Thomas that was read as agreed evidence did not in fact accord to other evidence that has not been disputed in the course of the case. I just wonder
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: why it was read out because it doesn't appear to meet the facts of the case, some of it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, apologies. We've obviously worked hard on editing the various witness statements into an agreed form. If we've missed that, I can only apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just didn't want there to be any confusion. For example, that the defendant was the designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. Well, again, I apologise for having missed that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that there were -- the statement, I don't have it in front of me. She couldn't recall there being any other babies in the unit at the time, but there were other babies in the unit, as the chart shows. Not only the unit, in that room, in nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just in future, I think if there are those matters that are clearly mistakes, unless someone actually wants them in order to undermine the credibility of the witness, it would be more helpful not to have them.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Noted. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. Because it just creates some potential confusion. I'm not going to say anything to the jury, but when I come to sum up the evidence I shall not refer to those errors.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, and we will be more alive to it in future.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's not a witness we request or rely upon, it just happened to be included in what was read out, but yes, we don't make any reference to what she said.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, exactly. Clearly she was mistaken, but this was a stressful event that was taking place and she was just confused.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. The jury, I think, have the undisputed evidence of who was where in the nursery at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: They have the slide with that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Which is the basis upon which we're all proceeding and the basis upon which they should proceed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
